Prediction target period: from 2024-06-26 to 2024-07-11. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the Consumer Price Index (CPI) for May 2024 was unchanged on a monthly basis, with the annual inflation rate easing to 3.3%, down from 3.4% in April. [11, 13] This moderation in inflation was a welcome sign for the Federal Reserve and led to increased expectations for an interest rate cut later in the year. [5, 1] The core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose 3.4% year-over-year, its slowest pace in over three years. [4, 5] A significant factor in the flat monthly headline number was a 2.0% decrease in the energy index, including a 3.6% drop in gasoline prices. [11] However, shelter costs continued to rise, increasing by 0.4% for the fourth consecutive month and tempering the overall decline in inflation. [5, 11] The softer inflation data contributed to a weakening of the U.S. dollar as it revived hopes for a potential rate cut by the Federal Reserve. <2> The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on June 7, 2024, that the economy added 272,000 nonfarm payroll jobs in May 2024, significantly surpassing economists' consensus forecasts, which ranged from 180,000 to 185,000. This robust job growth was led by gains in health care, government, and leisure and hospitality. The stronger-than-expected report, combined with an increase in average hourly earnings, dampened expectations for a near-term interest rate cut by the Federal Reserve. However, the report also presented a mixed view of the labor market, as the unemployment rate unexpectedly rose to 4.0%, its highest level since January 2022. The labor force participation rate also declined slightly to 62.5%. The strong jobs data led to a strengthening of the U.S. dollar, which in turn contributed to a weakening of the Korean Won. <3> The Institute for Supply Management (ISM) reported that the Manufacturing PMI® for May 2024 was 48.7%, a decrease of 0.5 percentage points from the 49.2% recorded in April. [2] This marked the second consecutive month of contraction in the manufacturing sector, and the decline occurred at a faster rate. [2] The report, which indicates a potential slowdown in economic activity, could influence the Federal Reserve's monetary policy and consequently affect the USD. <4> On May 31, 2024, the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) released its report for April 2024, indicating that personal income increased by $65.3 billion, or 0.3%. During the same period, personal consumption expenditures (PCE) rose by $39.1 billion, a 0.2% increase. The PCE price index, a critical inflation measure for the Federal Reserve, climbed 0.3% month-over-month and 2.7% year-over-year. The core PCE price index, which excludes volatile food and energy costs, saw a 0.2% monthly rise and a 2.8% annual increase. These figures, showing persistent inflation, were seen by analysts as likely to reinforce the Federal Reserve's cautious approach toward interest rate reductions, potentially supporting the value of the U.S. dollar. <5> On May 30, 2024, the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) issued its "second" estimate for the first-quarter 2024 U.S. Gross Domestic Product (GDP), revising the annualized growth rate down to 1.3%. [1] This was a decrease from the "advance" estimate of 1.6%. [1] The downward revision was primarily a result of lower-than-previously-estimated consumer spending. [1] This indication of a slowing economy was noted to have put some downward pressure on the U.S. dollar. <6> In April 2024, U.S. retail sales remained unexpectedly flat, showing no change from the previous month, a figure that fell short of the 0.4% increase economists had anticipated. This stagnation, following a revised 0.6% increase in March, was seen as an indication of cooling consumer spending. The data, released by the Commerce Department, put downward pressure on the U.S. dollar as it suggested a potential slowdown in economic growth. <7> The Institute for Supply Management (ISM) announced that its Services Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) registered 49.4% for April 2024, a 2 percentage point decrease from the March reading of 51.4%. [5] This marked the first time the services sector entered into contraction territory since December 2022, ending a 15-month period of growth. [5] The drop was unexpected by economists, who had forecasted a slight increase to 52 percent. [4] This weaker-than-expected economic data, combined with a U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics report of a lower-than-anticipated increase in total nonfarm payroll employment of 175,000 in April, led to increased speculation that the Federal Reserve might implement an interest rate cut. [4] The combination of these reports resulted in a weakening of the U.S. dollar and a rise in stock markets, as investors anticipated a cooling economy. [4] <8> The U.S. economy added 175,000 jobs in April 2024, a figure significantly lower than the forecasted 243,000 to 241,000. [1] This unexpectedly slower job growth, the weakest since October 2023, was accompanied by a slight increase in the unemployment rate to 3.9%. [1, 2] The report, released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, also indicated a moderation in wage growth, with average hourly earnings rising 0.2% for the month and 3.9% over the past year. [1, 3] The weaker-than-expected labor market data led to a temporary decline in the U.S. dollar, as it increased market expectations for a potential interest rate cut by the Federal Reserve. [3] In response to the softer U.S. economic data, the Korean Won strengthened. Job gains were most notable in the health care, social assistance, and transportation and warehousing sectors. [3, 6] Revisions to previous months' data showed that employment gains in February and March combined were 22,000 lower than initially reported. [3, 6] <9> The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that nonfarm business sector labor productivity increased by a preliminary estimate of 0.3% in the first quarter of 2024; This was accompanied by a 4.7% increase in unit labor costs; reflecting a 5.0% rise in hourly compensation <10> The Institute for Supply Management (ISM) reported that the Manufacturing PMI® for April 2024 registered 49.2%, a decrease of 1.1 percentage points from the March reading of 50.3%. [2, 5] This reading indicated a return to contraction for the manufacturing sector after one month of expansion, which had followed 16 consecutive months of contraction. [5] A notable component of the report was the Prices Index, which surged by 5.1 percentage points to 60.9%, its highest level since June 2022. [5] This increase in raw material prices signaled potential inflationary pressures, which could complicate future interest rate decisions by the Federal Reserve. The report, which was released on May 1, 2024, also showed that the New Orders and Employment Indexes moved into contraction territory, while the Production Index remained in expansion, though at a slower rate. [5]

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On Friday, October 4, 2024, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) is scheduled to release the Employment Situation Summary for September 2024. A survey of 25 economists by FactSet predicted a median increase of 140,000 in total nonfarm payrolls and for the unemployment rate to hold steady at 4.2%. <2> The U.S. Transportation Command (USTRANSCOM) and the Republic of Korea renewed their Mutual Airlift Support Agreement (MASA) in August 2024, enhancing airlift capabilities in the Indo-Pacific region. [2] The original agreement, which was signed in July 2004, facilitates coordination between the U.S. and Korean air forces, including their contracted civilian aircraft, during contingencies on the Korean Peninsula. [2, 3] The renewed MASA includes updated arrangements that specify steps for command and control to improve military coordination and operational efficiency. [2, 3] In the year leading up to the renewal, the agreement was utilized in key operations, such as the Korea Rotation Force '24, which repositioned hundreds of personnel and thousands of pounds of equipment. [2, 3] <3> On September 17, 2024, the U.S. Census Bureau announced that advance estimates for U.S. retail and food services sales for August 2024 were $710.8 billion, a 0.1% increase from the prior month. [2, 3] This slight increase surpassed market expectations of a 0.2% decline, indicating continued resilience in consumer spending. [3] Total sales for the June to August 2024 period rose 2.3% compared to the same period in the previous year. [1, 3] Year-over-year, sales were up 2.1% from August 2023. [2, 7] <4> On September 12, 2024, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the Producer Price Index (PPI) for final demand, covering the month of August 2024, increased by 0.2% on a seasonally adjusted basis. This rise was attributed to a 0.4% increase in prices for final demand services, while the index for final demand goods remained unchanged. On an unadjusted basis, the final demand index saw a 1.7% increase for the 12-month period ending in August. <5> On September 11, 2024, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics announced that the Consumer Price Index (CPI) for All Urban Consumers registered a 2.5% year-over-year increase for the period ending in August 2024. This represented the smallest annual rise in inflation since February 2021. The core CPI, which omits the more volatile food and energy sectors, increased by 3.2% over the same 12-month period. Specifically, July imports were $345.4 billion, a $7.1 billion increase from June, while July exports were $266.6 billion, which was $1.3 billion more than June exports. [4, 5, 6] This marked the fourth consecutive month of contraction for the U.S. manufacturing sector, and at a more rapid pace. [4, 5] Key sub-indexes also remained in contraction territory, with the New Orders Index registering 47.4 percent and the Production Index at 45.9 percent. [4, 6] The Employment Index saw a significant decrease to 43.4 percent, while the Prices Index indicated an increase in raw material prices for the seventh consecutive month, registering 52.9 percent. Specifically, manufacturing output decreased by 0.4% and mining output fell by 0.3%, while utilities output increased by 3.3%. This figure also represents a 5.2% unadjusted year-over-year increase from April 2024. The report, a key indicator of consumer spending, provides an early look at economic activity at the beginning of the second quarter. Total sales for April 2025 were estimated at $724.1 billion. <3> On May 1, 2025, the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) issued a finding and a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) identifying the Cambodia-based Huione Group as a financial institution of primary money laundering concern. [1, 2, 7] The action, taken under Section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act, proposes to sever the conglomerate's access to the U.S. financial system. [2, 7] FinCEN's investigation found that between August 2021 and January 2025, Huione Group laundered at least $4 billion in illicit proceeds. [1, 2, 7] The funds were linked to two primary illicit activities: laundering proceeds from cyber heists carried out by North Korean actors, including the Lazarus Group, and facilitating funds for transnational criminal organizations in Southeast Asia perpetrating digital asset investment scams, commonly known as "pig butchering." [2, 4, 5] Of the total laundered amount, FinCEN identified at least $37 million from North Korean cyber heists, $36 million from convertible virtual currency (CVC) investment scams, and $300 million from other cyber scams. This growth was largely driven by the popularity of U.S. equity-based products, including derivatives such as leveraged, inverse, and covered calls. In its official statement, the Committee noted that while economic activity continued to expand at a solid pace and labor market conditions remained strong, inflation was still somewhat elevated. The statement notably removed a previous reference to inflation having made progress toward the Committee's 2 percent goal, a change that some traders interpreted as a "hawkish" signal. Officials indicated they would carefully assess incoming data, the evolving economic outlook, and the balance of risks before making future adjustments. The decision was also influenced by uncertainty surrounding the potential economic impact of policies from the new Trump administration, such as tariffs and immigration, which could be inflationary. <9> A retrospective analysis by UBS indicated that the Korean won (KRW) had its worst performance in 2024 since the 2008 Global Financial Crisis. [4] The currency depreciated by 13% against the US dollar over the year, with a significant three-quarters of this decline occurring in the fourth quarter. [4] Factors contributing to this underperformance included the Kospi's relative weakness, a tightening Korea-US 10-year yield spread, a slow manufacturing and export cycle, resident capital outflows, and domestic political issues late in the year. [4] Other reports from late 2024 and early 2025 also highlighted the won's significant depreciation, citing geopolitical turmoil and diverging interest rate policies between the US and South Korea as key drivers. [5, 7, 8] <10> On January 10, 2025, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the American economy added 256,000 jobs in December 2024, a figure significantly above market expectations. Concurrently, the unemployment rate decreased to 4.1 percent from 4.2 percent in the previous month. The job gains were primarily driven by growth in the private education, health services, retail trade, and leisure and hospitality sectors. This report concluded a year that saw the addition of approximately 2.2 million jobs to the U.S. economy.

As part of the deal, China committed to suspend for one year its newly announced export controls on rare earth elements and other critical minerals, and to issue general licenses for the export of materials like gallium, germanium, antimony, and graphite to U.S. end users. In return, the United States agreed to refrain from imposing new import tariffs and to lower existing tariffs related to fentanyl precursors from 20% to 10%. The agreement also includes Chinese commitments to purchase a significant amount of U.S. agricultural products, such as soybeans. Policymakers cited increasing downside risks to employment as a key reason for the move, aiming to stabilize a weakening labor market. The partnership also focuses on developing advanced wireless networks like 6G, strengthening research security to protect technology, and ensuring resilient supply chains for pharmaceuticals and biotechnology. The agreement stipulates that South Korea will invest $350 billion in the U.S. in exchange for a reduction in U.S. tariffs on South Korean automobiles and auto parts from 25% to 15%. The investment is structured as $200 billion in cash installments, with an annual cap of $20 billion, and an additional $150 billion allocated for shipbuilding cooperation through direct investments and loans. The deal followed months of negotiations, which included a preliminary agreement announced during President Lee's visit to Washington in July 2025. A key point of contention was the structure of the investment. The U.S. initially pushed for a large, upfront cash payment, but South Korea expressed concerns that this would negatively impact the won-dollar exchange rate. The final agreement mitigates these concerns by structuring the investment as $200 billion in phased cash installments, capped at $20 billion annually, and $150 billion for cooperation in the shipbuilding industry. As part of the deal, South Korea committed to a $350 billion investment in the United States, which includes $200 billion in direct cash investments and $150 billion toward the U.S. shipbuilding industry. To mitigate this, negotiations are focused on structuring the package as a balanced mix of direct investments, loans, and guarantees. The package is reported to consist of $200 billion in cash investments and $150 billion in shipbuilding cooperation, with investments planned to proceed within an annual limit of $20 billion to minimize market impact. This approach is intended to mitigate potential shocks to Seoul's foreign exchange market that could result from a large, upfront deployment of funds. Koo confirmed that U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent understands this risk and is discussing the matter internally. While a currency swap has been discussed as a potential financial safety measure, Koo emphasized that its necessity and scale are entirely dependent on the final investment structure, stating it may not be needed at all or could be arranged on a smaller scale. The interview took place on the sidelines of the APEC Finance Ministers' Meeting in Incheon, South Korea. <10> On October 15, 2025, South Korean and U.S. officials, including South Korea's Deputy Prime Minister for Economic Affairs Koo and U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessant, held negotiations regarding a $350 billion U.S. investment fund. Discussions focused on creating a fund structure that would mitigate the negative impact on the South Korean foreign exchange market. The South Korean side expressed concern that a large, short-term 'pre-payment' in U.S. dollars could cause a sharp depreciation of the won and sought to extend the investment period. These negotiations continued on October 16 with other high-level officials, including South Korea's presidential policy chief Yongbum Kim and U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Rutnick.
